clue.text: Passed down from Lancaster?

indicators.note: what is passed down is made from the city's name, its letters reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A question about what was inherited from a city in Lancashire, or from the royal House of Lancaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'from' signals that the answer is made out of LANCASTER's letters. Lancaster is an English city and also a royal house, which suits the idea of inheritance.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ancestral has been inherited, handed down through the generations of a family.

clue.text: Old guard going after first prize

indicators.note: the guard's word follows the first piece, so it comes second in the answer

parts.note: A is first-class, top grade, as in A1
ward is an archaic word for guard or watch, as in watch and ward

explanation.surface: A retired sentry runs off after winning first prize.
explanation.definitionFit: An award is a prize given in recognition of an achievement.

clue.text: Non-U physicist admitted embracing a South American

indicators.note: Non- placed before U says that the letter U is taken away from the physicist's name

parts.note: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb was the French physicist after whom the unit of electric charge is named

indicators.note: embracing means the word for admitted wraps itself round the single letter

parts.note: admitted means let in, so IN

explanation.surface: A scientist who is not upper class has been let in, hugging someone from South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-U' looks like the British class tag for not upper class; here it means take the U out of the physicist's name, giving COLOMB.
explanation.definitionFit: A Colombian is a native or citizen of Colombia, a country in South America.

clue.text: Anglers got flounder? What a blow!

indicators.note: to flounder is to thrash about clumsily, so the preceding letters are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: Fishermen hooked a flounder, an exclamation of how impressive that is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flounder' looks like the flatfish the anglers caught; it is the verb, signalling an anagram of ANGLERS GOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong gale is a very high wind on the Beaufort scale, which is certainly quite a blow.

clue.text: Sound heard at door right next to empty apartment — thrice

indicators.note: next to places the abbreviation for right beside what follows it

parts.note: apartment emptied of its inside letters leaves its first and last, and 'thrice' asks for this piece three times
apartment emptied of its inside letters leaves its first and last, and 'thrice' asks for this piece three times
apartment emptied of its inside letters leaves its first and last, and 'thrice' asks for this piece three times

explanation.surface: A knock at the front door, heard right beside an unoccupied flat three times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrice' says the emptied apartment, its outer letters AT, is used three times after R.
explanation.definitionFit: Rat-a-tat imitates the sound of repeated knocking on a door.

clue.text: Overture, one of several, alone or in concert

indicators.note: in concert suggests the letters working together in a new arrangement, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A piece of orchestral music that can be played on its own or at a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: Beethoven wrote several overtures for his opera Fidelio, named after its heroine; three of them are numbered, which is why the clue says 'one of several'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leonora overtures are the numbered overtures Beethoven wrote for Fidelio, whose heroine is called Leonore.

clue.text: Necktie — one from Paisley, say

parts.note: one gives the article A
Paisley is a town in Scotland, so someone from there is an example of a Scot

explanation.surface: A tie that comes from Paisley, the Scottish town famous for its patterned fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: Paisley is a Scottish town that gave its name to a swirling fabric pattern, so 'Necktie' and 'Paisley' look like one picture.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot is a broad necktie or cravat, named after the Berkshire racecourse.

clue.text: Long or short account? What's up?

parts.note: AC is the usual short form of account

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: eh is an interjection asking what was said

explanation.surface: A question about whether to give a long or a short report, and what is going on.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache for something is to long for it, yearn for it.

clue.text: Look at the mileometer

definitions.meaning: British slang for to notice or look at them
the dial showing distance travelled in a car is informally called the ..., as in miles on the ...

explanation.definitionFit: Clock is slang both for noticing something and for a car's distance recorder, the odometer.

clue.text: Roget? He's among the stars

indicators.note: among puts the two-word phrase inside the constellation's name

parts.note: Taurus, the Bull, is a constellation and sign of the zodiac
taken as written, the letters of He's

explanation.surface: A question asking whether Roget is someone who moves among celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the stars' suggests celebrities, which fits 'among'; it is a constellation of the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mark Roget compiled the famous word-finder, so his name stands for that reference book; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: A doctor takes in 50% less as a psychiatrist

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: takes in means the doctor's abbreviation contains the piece that follows
50% means only half of the word less is used, its first two letters

explanation.surface: A doctor accepts half the payment and works as a psychiatrist.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of 'less' gives LE, its first two letters. Alfred Adler was a colleague of Freud's before founding his own school.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Adler was an Austrian psychiatrist, founder of individual psychology.

clue.text: Delicious nipper takes part

parts.note: a tooth nips or bites, so it can be called a nipper
some means a part of something, as in have some cake

explanation.surface: A tasty little child takes a share of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nipper' looks like British slang for a small child; here it is something that nips, a TOOTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Toothsome food is tasty and appetizing, pleasing to eat.

clue.text: Government formed with a Tory leader in control

indicators.note: in places the article and the leading letter inside the word for government

parts.note: dominion means sovereignty, government or rule

indicators.note: leader means only the first letter of Tory is used

explanation.surface: A government is set up with a Conservative leader in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: A and T (the Tory leader) go inside DOMINION.
explanation.definitionFit: Domination is the exercise of power or control over others.

clue.text: Fine artist depicting lady's fingers

parts.note: OK means fine, all right
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword stand-in for an artist

explanation.surface: A talented painter makes a picture of a woman's hands.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady's fingers is a British name for the vegetable, so the definition is fair though it reads as a woman's hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Okra pods are also known as lady's fingers or gumbo, from their long tapering shape.

clue.text: Believe in people initially

definitions.meaning: in Cockney rhyming slang the phrase for the first couple rhymes with believe, as in would you believe it
the first man and woman in Genesis were the first people, the people at the start

explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang swaps a word for a phrase that rhymes with it; here the biblical couple stands for believe.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the first humans were the couple in Eden, and in rhyming slang their names mean believe.

clue.text: Female saint in place of captain at head of troops

parts.note: a ship's captain commands from the bridge

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of troops is taken

explanation.surface: A woman takes the captain's place at the front of the soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captain' looks military beside 'troops'; it is a ship's captain, whose post is the BRIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Bridget, also Brigid, is a patron saint of Ireland; Bridget of Sweden is another.

clue.text: Point of reference for boys outside church

indicators.note: outside means the two names go round the abbreviation for church

parts.note: Ben and Mark are both boys' names
Ben and Mark are both boys' names

explanation.surface: A reference point for youngsters standing outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, 'boys', supplies two different names, one each side of the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A benchmark is a standard or point of reference against which things are measured.

clue.text: Give Cockney a place in Hampshire

indicators.note: the London Cockney accent drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: to hand over is to give

explanation.surface: Grant a Londoner a spot somewhere in Hampshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech drops initial H, so HAND OVER becomes ANDOVER. Hampshire is a county in southern England, and Andover is a town in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Andover is a market town in Hampshire, in southern England.

clue.text: Game French count

definitions.meaning: a card game, a form of blackjack or pontoon, played to reach twenty-one
the French for twenty-one, a number in counting

explanation.definitionFit: Vingt-et-un is French for twenty-one, and is also the name of the card game pontoon or blackjack.

clue.text: Puzzle no longer translated?

definitions.meaning: to puzzle someone is to baffle or perplex them
the clue words rendered into French or Latin would be ..., no more

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the loose translation: strictly French 'no longer' is ne ... plus, but the setter reads the answer as two foreign words.
explanation.definitionFit: To nonplus someone is to bewilder them so they do not know how to respond.

clue.text: Believe in a bird

definitions.meaning: to ... a story is to believe it unquestioningly
a small migratory bird with a forked tail

explanation.definitionFit: Swallow means to accept a claim without question, and is also a fork-tailed migrating bird.

clue.text: About mid-November, change for American bonds

indicators.note: About means the coins go around the middle letters

parts.note: cents are the small change of the US dollar

indicators.note: mid means the middle two letters of November are taken

explanation.surface: Around the middle of November, an American exchanges cash for bonds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bonds' looks like financial bonds beside 'change'; it is the verb, sticks together. 'mid' takes EM from the middle of November.
explanation.definitionFit: To cement things is to bind or stick them firmly together.

clue.text: Portion of butter one served with tea bread

parts.note: cha, or char, is British slang for tea
a pat is a small flat portion of butter
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A pat of butter was served with a cup of tea and some bread.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade runs in answer order: CHA, then PAT, then I, though the clue names the butter first.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapati is a flat unleavened bread of South Asian cooking.

clue.text: Song for that man on the radio?

indicators.note: on the radio means words heard rather than seen, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: him refers to that man

explanation.surface: A song dedicated to a particular man being broadcast on the radio.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymn is a religious song of praise, sung in church.

clue.text: Africans as puzzled as I am

indicators.note: puzzled suggests the following words are confused, their letters jumbled

explanation.surface: People from Africa are as baffled as the speaker is.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'as' is a link; the fodder is AS I AM.
explanation.definitionFit: The Masai are a pastoral people of Kenya and Tanzania in East Africa.

clue.text: Ancient, as a settlement for ancient people

indicators.note: a settlement is something sorted out or arranged, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something old, as a village, suited ancient inhabitants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settlement' looks like a village, which suits the ancient people; it signals an anagram of ANCIENT AS A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canaanites were the people of Canaan, the ancient land of the Levant in the Bible.

clue.text: Cavity walls in useless bridge?

indicators.note: the answer forms a bridge spanning the gaps between the printed words, joining their end and start

explanation.surface: A question about the gap in walls on a bridge that serves no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cavity walls' looks like a building phrase, but 'Cavity' alone is the definition; the answer spans wallS IN USeless.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinus is a hollow cavity, especially one of the air spaces in the skull bones.

clue.text: Worry about appearing in newspaper

indicators.note: appearing in means the short word for about goes inside the paper's initials

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Concern about a story that has appeared in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The FT is the Financial Times, a British daily paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret is to worry or be anxious about something.

clue.text: Commonwealth country with a large interior

indicators.note: interior means the article and the abbreviation for large go inside the country

parts.note: Austria is a country in central Europe
L is the standard abbreviation for large, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A Commonwealth nation whose interior is vast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonwealth country' reads as one phrase; the definition is just 'Commonwealth', the nation's official title, and 'country' is AUSTRIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The nation's official name is the Commonwealth of Australia, so the word alone names it.

clue.text: Dined in college by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the pronunciation, not the spelling, is what counts here

parts.note: Eton College is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Had a meal in a college, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is an elite English boarding school, formally Eton College.
explanation.definitionFit: Eaten is the past participle of eat, as in have dined, so it stands for dined.

clue.text: Drink knocked back — setback for artist

indicators.note: knocked back means the drink's name is read in reverse

parts.note: milk is a drink
the back of the word set, its final letter

explanation.surface: A drink is downed, and that is a reverse for the painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' looks like drinking but reverses MILK; 'setback' is the back of 'set', T.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Klimt was an Austrian symbolist painter, known for The Kiss.

clue.text: Insects on holiday, having abandoned a nest

parts.note: Whit, or Whitsun, is a Christian festival and British holiday

indicators.note: abandoned means wild and unrestrained, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: Insects go on holiday after leaving their nest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned a nest' looks like leaving home; it is an anagram of A NEST, giving EANTS. Whit is Whitsun, a British holiday seven weeks after Easter.
explanation.definitionFit: White ants is a common name for termites, insects that build large nests.
